scenario.student_message: Did that. For 9–10 vs 14–15: `request.start < b.end` is 14 < 10, false. But `request.end > b.start` is 15 > 9, true. And since I was joining them with an or, one true was enough to push it into conflicts. tutor_response: That's exactly it, and your reasoning is the right reasoning, not just a lucky operator swap. Two intervals overlap only when each one begins before the other one ends — both facts have to be true simultaneously, so the two comparisons form a conjunction. With the or, you were asking a much weaker question, and it's worth seeing how weak: for any two intervals that don't overlap, one of them lies entirely after the other, and whichever one that is will satisfy one of your two comparisons. So the or version returns true for essentially every pair, which is why it looked like your room filter was the only thing doing any work. A nice way to double-check this kind of predicate is to write the negation instead, since non-overlap is easy to state: either the request ends at or before the booking starts, or the booking ends at or before the request starts. Negate that with De Morgan and you land precisely on the pair of conditions you now have, with the strict inequalities intact — which is also why back-to-back bookings like 10–11 against 9–10 correctly come back clean, since touching endpoints aren't shared time. Your 9:30–10:30 test is the important one to keep, because it catches the partial-overlap case that a naive containment check would miss.

Each `next()` hands back element[i] and increments i. When you delete an element at or before position i, everything after it slides one slot to the left, but the iterator's counter keeps marching forward — so the element that just slid into the vacated slot is stepped straight over.
